# When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling

###### Abstract

Scaling test-time compute through extended chains of thought has become a dominant paradigm for improving large language model reasoning. However, existing research implicitly assumes that longer thinking always yields better results. This assumption remains largely unexamined.
We systematically investigate how the marginal utility of additional reasoning tokens changes as compute budgets increase. We find that marginal returns diminish substantially at higher budgets and that models exhibit “overthinking”, where extended reasoning is associated with abandoning previously correct answers.
Furthermore, we show that optimal thinking length varies across problem difficulty, suggesting that uniform compute allocation is suboptimal. Our cost-aware evaluation framework reveals that stopping at moderate budgets can reduce computation significantly while maintaining comparable accuracy.

## 1 Introduction

Scaling inference-time compute through lengthy chains of thought has achieved remarkable success on mathematical reasoning benchmarks ([DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Muennighoff et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)). Recent work has established that test-time compute scaling can be more effective than model scaling for many tasks ([Snell et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib7)). The prevailing assumption in this line of research is straightforward: more thinking leads to better answers. Models are encouraged to reason longer, with performance curves consistently showing accuracy improvements as token budgets increase. Yet the assumption that thinking length and answer quality are monotonically related has never been systematically examined.

We challenge this assumption by drawing an analogy from economics: the law of diminishing marginal returns. Just as additional units of input eventually yield smaller increments of output, additional tokens of reasoning may provide progressively less benefit. More critically, extended thinking might even be harmful. A model could “overthink” a problem, second-guessing a correct initial intuition and ultimately arriving at a wrong answer ([Chen et al., 2024a](#bib.bib17)). This phenomenon would have significant implications for how we deploy and evaluate test-time scaling systems.

Understanding when to stop thinking is practically important for two reasons. First, compute costs are substantial: generating 8,000 tokens costs 16×\times more than generating 500 tokens. If much of this extended reasoning provides minimal benefit, resources are being wasted. Second, if overthinking degrades performance on certain problems, then adaptive stopping strategies could simultaneously reduce costs and improve accuracy.

To investigate these questions, we conduct a systematic study of marginal utility in test-time compute scaling. We evaluate models across a wide range of compute budgets, measuring not just final accuracy but the incremental benefit of additional reasoning. We track individual problems through their reasoning trajectories, identifying “flip events” where answers change from correct to incorrect. Based on these analyses, we characterize when overthinking occurs and explore early-stopping strategies. In summary, we:

Provide a comprehensive analysis of marginal utility in test-time compute scaling, introducing flip event tracking to measure when extended reasoning helps versus hurts.

Identify and quantify the “overthinking” phenomenon, where extended reasoning is associated with models abandoning correct answers.

Introduce cost-aware evaluation metrics and propose that researchers report efficiency frontiers alongside accuracy curves.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Test-Time Scaling

Scaling inference compute has emerged as a powerful paradigm complementing training-time scaling ([Snell et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Wu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib7); [Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)). Methods include searching over generations, sampling multiple completions, and training models to produce extended reasoning chains ([OpenAI, 2024](#bib.bib15); [DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Muennighoff et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)). Recent surveys have comprehensively examined the landscape of long chain-of-thought reasoning ([Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Sui et al., 2025](#bib.bib13); [Zhou et al., 2025b](#bib.bib23); [Zhou and Zhou, 2025](#bib.bib26)). These works consistently report accuracy improvements with compute, but do not systematically examine marginal returns or the possibility of overthinking.

### 2.2 Overthinking in LLMs

Recent work has begun to identify the “overthinking” phenomenon in reasoning models. [Chen et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib11) first documented that o1-like models consume excessive tokens on simple problems with minimal accuracy benefit. [Wu et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib12) demonstrated that task accuracy follows an inverted U-shaped curve with chain-of-thought length. Several concurrent works examine related aspects: [Srivastava et al. (2025)](#bib.bib18) study accuracy-verbosity trade-offs on basic math tasks through an “overthinking score” metric; [Ghosal et al. (2025)](#bib.bib19) question test-time scaling effectiveness and propose parallel thinking as an alternative; [Lu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib24) survey adaptive test-time compute methods; and [Zhang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib20) use structural analysis tools to identify “over-verification” and “over-exploration” patterns. Our work complements these efforts by introducing flip event tracking to measure individual-problem answer changes, difficulty-stratified analysis revealing that easy problems overthink at 2K tokens versus 8K for hard problems, and a cost-aware evaluation framework with tunable λ\lambda parameter for accuracy-compute trade-offs.

### 2.3 Selective Prediction

Our work connects to selective classification ([Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017](#bib.bib4)) and selective question answering ([Kamath et al., 2020](#bib.bib5); [Zhou et al., 2025a](#bib.bib21); [Zhou et al., 2025c](#bib.bib22)), which allow models to abstain when uncertain. [Jurayj et al. (2025)](#bib.bib14) recently applied these ideas to test-time scaling, showing that confidence thresholds improve performance under risk. We extend this perspective by considering compute costs rather than response risks.

### 2.4 Efficient Inference

Prior work on efficient inference focuses on model compression, early exit ([Schwartz et al., 2020](#bib.bib9)), and speculative decoding ([Leviathan et al., 2023](#bib.bib8)). Our work suggests a complementary approach: adaptive reasoning length based on problem characteristics and overthinking detection.

## 3 Methods

We investigate how the benefit of additional reasoning changes as compute budgets increase. Our analysis focuses on three aspects: marginal utility measurement, flip event detection, and overthinking indicators. We describe each below:

### 3.1 Compute Budget

Following [Muennighoff et al. (2025)](#bib.bib2), we quantify a model’s compute budget by the number of tokens in its reasoning trace. We use budget forcing to control reasoning length: we append “Wait” tokens if the model attempts to conclude early, and force-decode the end-of-thinking delimiter once the budget is reached. We evaluate budgets in the range [500,16000][500,16000] tokens, with increments of 500 tokens.

# Inference-time scaling on Red Hat AI: Improving model reliability

### How its\_hub helps teams improve model accuracy and reliability at inference time

Language models offer impressive capabilities, but they're not always consistent. The same prompt can produce different answers, different reasoning paths, or different tool choices across runs. This variability might be acceptable in casual use, but it matters much more when models are used in products, enterprise workflows, and agentic systems. In those settings, reliability matters as much as raw capability.

Inference-time scaling (ITS) offers a practical way to address this inconsistency. Instead of accepting a single generation, ITS uses additional compute at runtime to generate multiple candidates, compare reasoning paths, and select the most accurate output before returning a final result. No retraining, no fine-tuning, no changes to model weights. The core insight: accuracy is an inference problem, not just a training problem.

That's the idea behind `its_hub`, [Red Hat AI](https://developers.redhat.com/products/red-hat-ai)'s open source framework for making these techniques usable in real systems. It supports methods such as best-of-N and self-consistency, as well as more advanced approaches like particle filtering and beam search, all in a common framework developers can apply incrementally.

`its_hub`

## What inference-time scaling is

ITS works by doing more during inference rather than relying on a single model call. An ITS system can generate several candidates, follow multiple reasoning paths, score outputs, or iteratively refine intermediate steps before returning a final answer.

This distinction matters because many model failures aren't caused by a lack of capability. Often the model can solve the task, but a single sampled response is brittle. A reasoning step drifts. The model returns a weaker answer over a more accurate one. It selects a plausible but wrong tool. An agent might choose the incorrect API call on one pass even though it was capable of the right choice from the start. Your models already know the answer; they don't always give it to you on the first try. Additional inference-time compute helps recover better outcomes by broadening the search space or improving the selection process.

This capability makes ITS applicable across a range of settings: improving convergence on correct answers for reasoning tasks, surfacing stronger candidates for generation tasks, and reducing the impact of any single noisy decision in agentic workflows. The tradeoff is real, but it's one that teams can choose to make selectively, applying more compute only where the problem justifies it.

## The enterprise case for inference-time scaling

Inference-time scaling matters now because the market has validated it and enterprise adoption demands it. Every major provider has shipped thinking-budget controls: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, DeepSeek, and NVIDIA all offer ways to allocate more inference-time compute for harder tasks. Inference-time compute scaling is a product category, not a research curiosity.

However, every provider's implementation is model-level: baked into one specific model, controlled by the provider's API. Customers who want ITS on their own models, on their own infrastructure, have no production option. That's the gap `its_hub` fills.

`its_hub`

The need is especially urgent for agentic workloads. Fewer than 10% of organizations have moved AI agents to production, and a primary blocker is reliability. Agents fail not because the underlying models lack capability, but because tool calling is unreliable. A single wrong tool call cascades through the entire workflow. ITS with consensus-based voting addresses this issue directly, turning unreliable tool selection into dependable automation.

ITS also gives teams a way to match compute to the demands of each task. Easy questions stay fast and cheap. Hard questions get the compute they deserve. This approach makes inference a configurable budget rather than a fixed cost, and means teams can improve accuracy without retraining, without API lock-in, and without changing the model itself.

## How its\_hub brings ITS into practice

`its_hub` packages practical inference-time scaling techniques into a consistent framework so teams can experiment, compare, and integrate them without building everything from scratch. This flexibility matters because ITS isn't monolithic. Different tasks call for different strategies, and `its_hub` supports this range rather than locking developers into a single pattern.

`its_hub`
`its_hub`

Today, `its_hub` offers two integration paths:

`its_hub`
`its_hub`

Both paths support `reward-hub` integration for feedback-driven scoring and selection, allowing developers to define custom evaluation functions and plug them directly into inference-time workflows.

`reward-hub`

Looking ahead, Red Hat is working to bring ITS into the Red Hat AI gateway as an infrastructure-level capability. The goal is to apply ITS to any model on any deployment through a single API header or parameter, with no code changes required. This work is underway and will be covered in future posts.

## Techniques available in its\_hub

Self-consistency generates multiple reasoning paths and selects the answer appearing most frequently across them, as shown in Figure 1. Rather than trusting a single trajectory, it lets agreement across runs influence the final result, which makes it particularly effective for reasoning tasks where the correct answer tends to recur even when individual traces vary.

![A prompt generates 5 responses, where majority voting selects "42" from 3 matching outputs over "37" and "41".](/sites/default/files/styles/article_floated/public/figure-1_36.png?itok=ryACA3me)

Best-of-N generates multiple candidate responses and uses a scoring mechanism to select the most accurate one, illustrated in Figure 2. Unlike self-consistency, which relies on consensus, best-of-N depends on an explicit evaluation signal, whether that's a large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge, a custom reward model, a validator, or other task-specific scoring logic.

![A reward model evaluates 5 candidate responses and selects Response 2 based on its top score of 9.1.](/sites/default/files/styles/article_floated/public/figure-2_32.png?itok=IE_gZOxI)

Hierarchical voting extends self-consistency to tool-calling workflows. When an agent needs to select and invoke tools, hierarchical voting samples multiple candidates in parallel and votes in stages: first on which tool to call, then on the arguments to pass. This two-level approach is especially effective for agentic tasks where the critical decision is not what text to generate, but what action to take.

Reward models act as lightweight evaluators scoring candidates based on criteria such as truthfulness, relevance, or domain fit. In best-of-N, they identify the top candidate; in self-consistency, they're optional but useful for resolving ties. Through `reward-hub` integration, developers can define custom scoring functions and plug them directly into inference-time workflows without touching the underlying model.

`reward-hub`

For workflows where intermediate reasoning steps matter, `its_hub` also supports particle filtering and beam search via its process reward model path. A process reward model scores each intermediate reasoning step rather than only the final output, making it possible to identify and prune weak trajectories before they reach a conclusion.

**Abstract:**Over the course of my PhD, large language models (LLMs) have undergone a fundamental shift in how they solve complex reasoning tasks. Early progress in this area was largely driven by scaling training data and model parameters. More recently, however, LLMs have increasingly relied on inference-time computation, such as retrieval, search, and extended chain-of-thought reasoning. This shift has enabled LLMs to tackle complex problems in math and science, but has also introduced challenges that limit the reliability of reasoning systems.

This thesis tackles three challenges that emerge from this paradigm shift. I first show that reasoning performance remains bottlenecked by the quality of the retriever, constrained by the availability of labeled data for training. To address this, I introduce a data-efficient retrieval approach for multi-hop reasoning that combines a lightweight unsupervised retriever with an LLM-based reranker. This method reduces reliance on supervised retriever training while achieving performance competitive with methods trained on substantially larger labeled datasets.

I then turn to verifying intermediate reasoning steps, a central challenge in settings such as search and training. I develop a scalable verification framework based on process-level supervision that alleviates the need for manual step-level annotations and more effectively scales inference-time techniques such as verifier-guided decoding. I further show that static discriminative verifiers become a bottleneck, as they cannot adaptively scale verification compute based on input complexity. To address this, I develop a generative process verifier that allocates additional inference-time computation to reason about correctness by generating verification chains.

Finally, I study failure modes that emerge when AI agents are evaluated using LLM judges. I show that agents can produce unfaithful reasoning traces that manipulate verifiers into accepting suboptimal actions as correct, revealing a failure mode in which agents game evaluation. Overall, these results show that while inference-time computation strengthens reasoning capabilities, it also introduces vulnerabilities that demand robust evaluation protocols.

Together, this thesis argues that verification is central—not auxiliary—to building trustworthy reasoning systems, and presents a unified framework for retrieval, verification, and evaluation in the era of inference-time compute.

# Categories of Inference-Time Scaling for Improved LLM Reasoning

### And an Overview of Recent Inference-Scaling Papers (Including Recursive Language Models)

[Sebastian Raschka, PhD](https://substack.com/@rasbt)

∙ Paid

Inference scaling has become one of the most effective ways to improve answer quality and accuracy in deployed LLMs.

The idea is straightforward. If we are willing to spend a bit more compute, and more time at inference time (when we use the model to generate text), we can get the model to produce better answers.

Every major LLM provider relies on some flavor of inference-time scaling today. And the academic literature around these methods has grown a lot, too.

Back in March, I wrote an overview of the inference scaling landscape and summarized some of the early techniques.

[#### The State of LLM Reasoning Model Inference

[Sebastian Raschka, PhD](https://substack.com/profile/27393275-sebastian-raschka-phd)

·

March 8, 2025

[Read full story](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/state-of-llm-reasoning-and-inference-scaling)](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/state-of-llm-reasoning-and-inference-scaling)

In this article, I want to take that earlier discussion a step further, group the different approaches into clearer categories, and highlight the newest work that has appeared over the past few months.

As part of drafting a full book chapter on inference scaling for *[Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch)](https://mng.bz/Nwr7)*, I ended up experimenting with many of the fundamental flavors of these methods myself. With hyperparameter tuning, this quickly turned into thousands of runs and a lot of thought and work to figure out which approaches should be covered in more detail in the chapter itself. (The chapter grew so much that I eventually split it into two, and both are now available in the early access program.)

PS: I am especially happy with how the chapter(s) turned out. It takes the base model from about 15 percent to around 52 percent accuracy, which makes it one of the most rewarding pieces of the book so far.

What follows here is a collection of ideas, notes, and papers that did not quite fit into the final chapter narrative but are still worth sharing.

I also plan to add more code implementations to the [bonus materials on GitHub](https://github.com/rasbt/reasoning-from-scratch) over time.

**Table of Contents (Overview)**

1. Inference-Time Scaling Overview
2. Chain-of-Thought Prompting
3. Self-Consistency
4. Best-of-N Ranking
5. Rejection Sampling with a Verifier
6. Self-Refinement
7. Search Over Solution Paths
8. Conclusions, Categories, and Combinations
9. Bonus: What Do Proprietary LLMs Use?

You can use the left-hand navigation bar in the article’s web view to jump directly to any section.

# 1. Inference-Time Scaling Overview

*Inference-time scaling* (also called *inference-compute scaling*, *test-time scaling*, or just *inference scaling*) is an umbrella term for methods that allocate more compute and time during inference to improve model performance.

This idea has been around for a long time, and one can think of ensemble methods in classic machine learning as an early example of inference-time scaling. I.e., using multiple models requires more compute resources but can give better results.

​Even in LLM contexts, this idea has been around for a long time. However, I remember it became particularly popular (again) when OpenAI showed an inference-time scaling and training plot in one of their o1 announcement blog articles last year ([Learning to Reason with LLMs](https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/)).

*Figure 1: Spending additional resources during inference (left) and training (right) generally improves the model’s accuracy.*

I think this figure, adapted from OpenAI’s [blog post](https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/), nicely captures the idea behind the two knobs we can use to improve LLMs. We can spend more resources during training (more data, bigger models, more or longer training stages) or inference.

Actually, in practice, it’s even better to do both at the same time: train a stronger model and use additional inference scaling to make it even better.

In this article, I only focus on the left part of the figure, inference-time scaling techniques, i.e., those training-free techniques that don’t change the model weights.

# [Revue de papier] Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference for Problem-Solving with Language Models

The paper titled "Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-optimal Inference for LLM Problem-solving" explores the relatively less discussed aspect of inference in large language models (LLMs), particularly focusing on how the inference process can be optimized in terms of compute efficiency and effectiveness. This paper, presented at the ICLR 2025 conference, addresses crucial trade-offs between model sizes, inference strategies, and the number of tokens generated during inference.

### Core Methodology

1. **Empirical Study**: The authors conducted extensive empirical experiments involving various LLM configurations. They studied several inference strategies including greedy search, best-of-n, majority voting, weighted voting, and two distinct tree search methodologies, particularly emphasizing a novel approach they call REward BAlanced SEarch (REBASE). The analyses were conducted across a variety of model sizes and compute budgets.
2. **Inference Scaling Laws**: The paper establishes inference scaling laws, which suggest that there is a predictable relationship between the amount of compute used during inference and the performance of the model. The authors provide empirical evidence indicating that increasing the compute during inference could lead to superior performance, akin to scaling training compute but focusing on the inference phase instead.
3. **Optimization Problem Formulation**:

   * The authors formally present the problem of compute-optimal inference as follows: Given a fixed compute budget C, determine the optimal model size N and the number of generated tokens T such that the error rate E(N,T;S) is minimized under the constraint that the compute required FLOPs(N,T;S)=C. This formulation allows for analyzing how to allocate compute resources effectively between model capacity and generated output.
4. **Evaluation Benchmarks**: The authors conducted evaluations using two primary benchmarks: MATH (measuring mathematical reasoning) and GSM8K (classifying simpler math problems). These benchmarks allowed for a standardized assessment of the models' reasoning capabilities.

### Inference Strategies Analyzed

* **Greedy Search**: The simplest strategy, selecting the highest probability token sequentially.
* **Best-of-n Sampling**: Generating multiple candidates and selecting the one with the best score given by a reward model.
* **Majority Voting and Weighted Majority Voting**: Aggregating answers from several generated outputs to enhance accuracy, where weights are used to express the quality of outputs.
* **Tree Search Approaches**: Including MCTS (Monte Carlo Tree Search) and REBASE, which utilize a structured approach to explore possibilities and prune unpromising paths.

### The Novel REBASE Algorithm

REBASE aims to improve on the deficiencies of MCTS by refining how nodes are evaluated and expanded based on a reward model. The critical distinction in REBASE is:

* **Cost Efficiency**: Unlike MCTS, which can consume substantial computation without guaranteeing high-quality outputs due to expensive tree rollouts, REBASE directly leverages a reward model to guide the expansion of nodes, thus eliminating unnecessary computations.
* **Dynamic Expansion**: The expansion of nodes in REBASE is controlled by normalized reward scores, which allows for a more targeted search process at each depth of the tree, optimizing candidate solution generation.

### Results and Findings

1. **Scale of Inference**: As shown in the experimental results, smaller models can outperform larger counterparts when using sophisticated inference strategies at fixed compute budgets. Specifically, the Llemma-7B model was found to provide similar or better results than Llemma-34B with halved compute in some cases.
2. **Compute-Efficiency**: The findings suggest that using more advanced inference strategies such as REBASE allows for significantly better performance metrics while consuming less compute. This efficiency plays a crucial role in practical applications where resources are limited.
3. **Saturation Observation**: While performance typically improves with increased compute, it was noted that this improvement may saturate, emphasizing that the changes in performance diminish after a certain point, reinforcing the need for refined inference strategies.

### Conclusion and Contribution

The authors highlight crucial implications for deploying LLMs in real-world scenarios where computational resources may be limited. They argue that leveraging smaller models with more effective inference algorithms can lead to better performance-cost trade-offs. This contribution marks a significant step toward examining and optimizing the inference phase of LLMs, ultimately guiding future research and practical applications of language models.

This paper sets a precedent for the necessity of investigating inference strategies comprehensively, urging the community to consider both model architecture and inference strategy in tandem for optimal performance.

# [Literature Review] Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference for Problem-Solving with Language Models

The paper titled "Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-optimal Inference for LLM Problem-solving" explores the relatively less discussed aspect of inference in large language models (LLMs), particularly focusing on how the inference process can be optimized in terms of compute efficiency and effectiveness. This paper, presented at the ICLR 2025 conference, addresses crucial trade-offs between model sizes, inference strategies, and the number of tokens generated during inference.

### Core Methodology

1. **Empirical Study**: The authors conducted extensive empirical experiments involving various LLM configurations. They studied several inference strategies including greedy search, best-of-n, majority voting, weighted voting, and two distinct tree search methodologies, particularly emphasizing a novel approach they call REward BAlanced SEarch (REBASE). The analyses were conducted across a variety of model sizes and compute budgets.
2. **Inference Scaling Laws**: The paper establishes inference scaling laws, which suggest that there is a predictable relationship between the amount of compute used during inference and the performance of the model. The authors provide empirical evidence indicating that increasing the compute during inference could lead to superior performance, akin to scaling training compute but focusing on the inference phase instead.
3. **Optimization Problem Formulation**:

   * The authors formally present the problem of compute-optimal inference as follows: Given a fixed compute budget C, determine the optimal model size N and the number of generated tokens T such that the error rate E(N,T;S) is minimized under the constraint that the compute required FLOPs(N,T;S)=C. This formulation allows for analyzing how to allocate compute resources effectively between model capacity and generated output.
4. **Evaluation Benchmarks**: The authors conducted evaluations using two primary benchmarks: MATH (measuring mathematical reasoning) and GSM8K (classifying simpler math problems). These benchmarks allowed for a standardized assessment of the models' reasoning capabilities.

### Inference Strategies Analyzed

* **Greedy Search**: The simplest strategy, selecting the highest probability token sequentially.
* **Best-of-n Sampling**: Generating multiple candidates and selecting the one with the best score given by a reward model.
* **Majority Voting and Weighted Majority Voting**: Aggregating answers from several generated outputs to enhance accuracy, where weights are used to express the quality of outputs.
* **Tree Search Approaches**: Including MCTS (Monte Carlo Tree Search) and REBASE, which utilize a structured approach to explore possibilities and prune unpromising paths.

### The Novel REBASE Algorithm

REBASE aims to improve on the deficiencies of MCTS by refining how nodes are evaluated and expanded based on a reward model. The critical distinction in REBASE is:

* **Cost Efficiency**: Unlike MCTS, which can consume substantial computation without guaranteeing high-quality outputs due to expensive tree rollouts, REBASE directly leverages a reward model to guide the expansion of nodes, thus eliminating unnecessary computations.
* **Dynamic Expansion**: The expansion of nodes in REBASE is controlled by normalized reward scores, which allows for a more targeted search process at each depth of the tree, optimizing candidate solution generation.

### Results and Findings

1. **Scale of Inference**: As shown in the experimental results, smaller models can outperform larger counterparts when using sophisticated inference strategies at fixed compute budgets. Specifically, the Llemma-7B model was found to provide similar or better results than Llemma-34B with halved compute in some cases.
2. **Compute-Efficiency**: The findings suggest that using more advanced inference strategies such as REBASE allows for significantly better performance metrics while consuming less compute. This efficiency plays a crucial role in practical applications where resources are limited.
3. **Saturation Observation**: While performance typically improves with increased compute, it was noted that this improvement may saturate, emphasizing that the changes in performance diminish after a certain point, reinforcing the need for refined inference strategies.

### Conclusion and Contribution

The authors highlight crucial implications for deploying LLMs in real-world scenarios where computational resources may be limited. They argue that leveraging smaller models with more effective inference algorithms can lead to better performance-cost trade-offs. This contribution marks a significant step toward examining and optimizing the inference phase of LLMs, ultimately guiding future research and practical applications of language models.

This paper sets a precedent for the necessity of investigating inference strategies comprehensively, urging the community to consider both model architecture and inference strategy in tandem for optimal performance.

# Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference for Problem-Solving with Language Models

[Yangzhen Wu](https://thu-wyz.github.io/)1,   [Zhiqing Sun](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~zhiqings/)2,   [Shanda Li](https://lithiumda.github.io/)2,   [Sean Welleck](https://wellecks.com/)2,   [Yiming Yang](http://www.cs.cmu.edu/~yiming/)2,

1Tsinghua University

2Carnegie Mellon University

[Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00724)     [Code](https://github.com/thu-wyz/inference_scaling)

## Abstract

While the scaling laws of large language models (LLMs) training have been extensively studied, optimal inference configurations of LLMs remain underexplored. We study **inference scaling laws** and **compute-optimal inference**, focusing on the trade-offs between model sizes and generating additional tokens with different inference strategies. As a first step towards understanding and designing compute-optimal inference methods, we studied cost-performance trade-offs for inference strategies such as greedy search, majority voting, best-of-$n$, weighted voting, and two different tree search algorithms, using different model sizes and compute budgets. Our findings indicate smaller models (e.g., Llemma-7B) can outperform larger models given the same computation budgets, and that smaller models paired with advanced inference algorithms yield Pareto-optimal cost-performance trade-offs. For instance, the Llemma-7B model, equipped with our novel tree search algorithm, consistently outperforms Llemma-34B with standard majority voting on the MATH benchmark across all FLOPs budgets. We hope these findings contribute to a broader understanding of inference scaling laws for LLMs.

## Inference-compute Scaling

More model parameters may lead to high performance on various tasks, but what about scaling the number of decoding tokens in inference? By measuring the amount of computation in FLOPs and studying model performance across different sizes and inference strategies as computation scales up, we can gain a deeper understanding of the effect of inference scaling.

---

  ![](./static/images/inference_scaling.png) 

The error rate versus computation budget(in Flops), we evaluate the Pythia models on the GSM8k dataset accross different model sizes.

   ![](./static/images/scaling.png) 

The *right* panel shows the model performances given inference FLOPs budgets. In particular, the three stars highlight the optimal model size under \(10^{12}\), \(10^{13}\), and \(10^{14}\) FLOPs, indicating that the optimal model size can vary given different budgets.

 

**Key findings:**

* Scaling inference compute by sampling more solutions leads to growing task performance.
* Across all scenarios, there is an eventual point at which the accuracy will reach a plateau, indicating that additional computational resources yield diminishing returns.
* The ideal model size varies depending on the available computational budget. Notably, smaller models tend to perform better when the compute budget is constrained.
* We also provide theoretical analysis which shows the upperbound and convergence rate in our paper, find more infomation in our paper!

## Compute-optimal Inference

In our paper, we also define the problem of compute-optimal inference, investigate the inference strategies that achieve high performance with a fixed compute budget.

 ![](./static/images/compute-optimal.png)   
 

comparison of compute-optimal inference and compute-optimal training

   ![](./static/images/gsm8k.png)   
 

rebase and sampling results on GSM8k

 

We introduce REward BAlanced SEarch (REBASE) which is Pareto optimal compared to sampling. We have the following findings:

* Sophisticated inference strategy like REBASE is compute-optimal.
* Smaller models equipped with advanced inference strategy outperforms larger ones.

# Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters (Paper)
## Yannic Kilcher
330000 subscribers
797 likes

### Description
31252 views
Posted: 5 Oct 2024
How can one best use extra FLOPS at test time?

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314

Abstract:
Enabling LLMs to improve their outputs by using more test-time computation is a critical step towards building generally self-improving agents that can operate on open-ended natural language. In this paper, we study the scaling of inference-time computation in LLMs, with a focus on answering the question: if an LLM is allowed to use a fixed but non-trivial amount of inference-time compute, how much can it improve its performance on a challenging prompt? Answering this question has implications not only on the achievable performance of LLMs, but also on the future of LLM pretraining and how one should tradeoff inference-time and pre-training compute. Despite its importance, little research attempted to understand the scaling behaviors of various test-time inference methods. Moreover, current work largely provides negative results for a number of these strategies. In this work, we analyze two primary mechanisms to scale test-time computation: (1) searching against dense, process-based verifier reward models; and (2) updating the model's distribution over a response adaptively, given the prompt at test time. We find that in both cases, the effectiveness of different approaches to scaling test-time compute critically varies depending on the difficulty of the prompt. This observation motivates applying a "compute-optimal" scaling strategy, which acts to most effectively allocate test-time compute adaptively per prompt. Using this compute-optimal strategy, we can improve the efficiency of test-time compute scaling by more than 4x compared to a best-of-N baseline. Additionally, in a FLOPs-matched evaluation, we find that on problems where a smaller base model attains somewhat non-trivial success rates, test-time compute can be used to outperform a 14x larger model.

## AI-Generated Summary

*   Large language models require two distinct inference phases: a prefill phase that processes input tokens in parallel and a decode phase that generates output tokens autoregressively and is memory-bound.
*   Key-value caching avoids recomputing attention tensors during decoding, but its memory footprint grows linearly with batch size and sequence length, limiting throughput for long-context workloads such as retrieval-augmented generation.
*   Model parallelism techniques including [pipeline parallelism](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo-framework/user-guide/latest/nemotoolkit/features/parallelisms.html#pipeline-parallelism), [tensor parallelism](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo-framework/user-guide/latest/nemotoolkit/features/parallelisms.html#tensor-parallelism:~:text=Tensor%20Parallelism-,%23,-Tensor%20Parallelism%20(TP), and sequence parallelism distribute model weights and activations across multiple GPUs to reduce per-device memory requirements.
*   Attention optimizations such as multi-query attention, grouped-query attention, and [FlashAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135) reduce key-value memory usage and improve GPU memory hierarchy utilization without changing model accuracy.
*   [PagedAttention](https://vllm.ai/) manages the key-value cache in fixed-size blocks stored non-contiguously, eliminating fragmentation from static over-provisioning and enabling larger batch sizes.
*   Model optimization techniques including quantization, structured sparsity, and knowledge distillation shrink model size and accelerate inference, while serving techniques such as in-flight batching and speculative inference increase GPU utilization and throughput.

### Next Steps

*   Deploy [NVIDIA NIM](https://developer.nvidia.com/nim) microservice containers to run prepackaged, validated inference workloads on NVIDIA GPUs.
*   Get started at [build.nvidia.com](http://build.nvidia.com/) to experiment with inference optimization techniques using production-grade code.

Stacking transformer layers to create large models results in better accuracies, few-shot learning capabilities, and even near-human emergent abilities on a wide range of language tasks. These foundation models are expensive to train, and they can be memory- and compute-intensive during inference (a recurring cost). The most popular [large language models (LLMs)](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/data-science/large-language-models/) today can reach tens to hundreds of billions of parameters in size and, depending on the use case, may require ingesting long inputs (or contexts), which can also add expense.For example, [retrieval-augmented generation](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/tag/retrieval-augmented-generation-rag/) (RAG) pipelines require putting large amounts of information into the input of the model, greatly increasing the amount of processing work the LLM has to do.

This post discusses the most pressing challenges in LLM inference, along with some practical solutions. Readers should have a basic understanding of [transformer architecture](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762.pdf) and the attention mechanism in general.

Developers can also explore these inference optimization techniques using open NVIDIA and community models—such as the [Nemotron 3 family](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-FP8)of open models—running on the open-source [TensorRT-LLM](https://github.com/CactusQ/TensorRT-LLM-Tutorial) library, available on GitHub. This makes it possible to experiment with real-world inference tradeoffs using production-grade code rather than abstract examples.

## Understanding LLM inference[](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/mastering-llm-techniques-inference-optimization/#understanding_llm_inference)

Most of the popular decoder-only LLMs (GPT-3, for example) are pretrained on the causal modeling objective, essentially as next-word predictors. These LLMs take a series of tokens as inputs, and generate subsequent tokens autoregressively until they meet a stopping criteria (a limit on the number of tokens to generate or a list of stop words, for example) or until it generates a special `<end>` token marking the end of generation. This process involves two phases: the prefill phase and the decode phase.

Note that _[tokens](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ai-tokens-explained/)_ are the atomic parts of language that a model processes. One token is approximately four English characters. All inputs in natural language are converted to tokens before inputting into the model.

### Prefill phase or processing the input[](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/mastering-llm-techniques-inference-optimization/#prefill_phase_or_processing_the_input)

In the prefill phase, the LLM processes the input tokens to compute the intermediate states (keys and values), which are used to generate the “first” new token. Each new token depends on all the previous tokens, but because the full extent of the input is known, at a high level this is a matrix-matrix operation that’s highly parallelized. It effectively saturates GPU utilization.

# Towards Efficient Multi-LLM Inference: Characterization and Analysis of LLM Routing and Hierarchical Techniques

###### Abstract

Recent progress in Language Models (LMs) has dramatically advanced the field of natural language processing (NLP), excelling at tasks like text generation, summarization, and question answering. However, their inference remains computationally expensive and energy-intensive, especially in settings with limited hardware, power, or bandwidth. This makes it difficult to deploy LMs in mobile, edge, or cost-sensitive environments. To address these challenges, recent approaches have introduced multi-LLM intelligent model selection strategies that dynamically allocate computational resources based on query complexity—using lightweight models for simpler queries and escalating to larger models only when necessary. This survey explores two complementary strategies for efficient LLM inference: (i) routing, which selects the most suitable model based on the query, and (ii) cascading or hierarchical inference (HI), which escalates queries through a sequence of models until a confident response is found. Both approaches aim to reduce computation by using lightweight models for simpler tasks while offloading only when needed. We provide a comparative analysis of these techniques across key performance metrics, discuss benchmarking efforts, and outline open challenges. Finally, we outline future research directions to enable faster response times, adaptive model selection based on task complexity, and scalable deployment across heterogeneous environments, making LLM-based systems more efficient and accessible for real-world applications.

###### Index Terms:

## I Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs), such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [[1](#bib.bib1)], Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) [[2](#bib.bib2)], and DeepSeek [[3](#bib.bib3)], have advanced machine understanding in Natural Language Processing (NLP) by achieving state-of-the-art performance in tasks such as text generation, question answering, and summarization. However, deploying these models at a large scale presents significant computational and financial challenges, particularly for small-to-medium-sized organizations and academic researchers who rely on pre-trained open-source models. While training LLMs demands substantial resources, inference costs remain a persistent concern, especially when high accuracy and responsiveness are required. Addressing these challenges necessitates strategies that optimize computational efficiency while maintaining performance.

Efficient LLM inference is particularly crucial for mobile and edge computing scenarios [[4](#bib.bib4)]. Currently, queries from mobile users are predominantly processed by large-scale cloud-based LLMs, including GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Llama. However, cloud-based inference incurs substantial costs due to the reliance on expensive Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) or Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and potential fees for API calls, limiting scalability and accessibility [[5](#bib.bib5), [6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7)]. An alternative is to shift inference closer to the user by utilizing edge servers equipped with open-source Small Language Models (SLMs) such as Llama 3.2 7B/11B [[8](#bib.bib8)], Phi-3 [[9](#bib.bib9)], and Mixtral 7B [[10](#bib.bib10)]. While this approach reduces latency and reliance on cloud infrastructure, it often compromises response quality [[11](#bib.bib11)]. Routing [[12](#bib.bib12)] and Hierarchical Inference (HI) [[13](#bib.bib13)] techniques address this trade-off by dynamically selecting the appropriate model based on task complexity, ensuring a balance between efficiency and performance.
These techniques prioritize efficient resource allocation by leveraging smaller, cost-effective models for initial processing and offloading to larger models only when necessary. Such adaptive strategies significantly reduce computational overhead while ensuring accuracy [[14](#bib.bib14)]. In recent years, advances in these techniques have demonstrated their potential for optimizing LLM deployment, highlighting the need for a comprehensive analysis of their capabilities and future research directions [[15](#bib.bib15)].

Routing mechanisms assign queries to the most suitable model out of multiple available models based on query complexities and model performances. For example, ZOOTER [[16](#bib.bib16)] employs reward-based metrics to assign queries to the most suitable models, optimizing both accuracy and cost. HI, on the other hand, employs a cascading 11
1
The terms HI and cascading have been used interchangeably in this paper. structure where all the queries are processed by lightweight models first, and complex queries will escalate to more powerful models only when additional processing is required. For instance, EcoAssistant [[13](#bib.bib13)] initially utilizes cost-effective models like GPT-3.5-turbo and escalates to GPT-4 when the response generated by the smaller model is not adequate. So in principle, these techniques can be defined as follows:

Routing: Routing systems dynamically assign queries to the most suitable model based on task complexity, accuracy requirements, and latency constraints. This approach ensures that tasks are handled by models that provide the best balance of cost and performance.

Cascading or HI: Cascading frameworks, on the other hand, prioritize smaller, cost-efficient models for simpler tasks and escalate to larger models only when necessary. This hierarchical inference process minimizes resource usage while maintaining output quality.

These adaptive strategies facilitate scalable, cost-effective inference, making them advantageous for real-time applications, resource-constrained environments, and high-demand NLP systems [[17](#bib.bib17), [18](#bib.bib18)].

### I-A Related Works

Efficient inference for LLMs has been a prominent area of research, with numerous surveys examining various techniques to improve performance, reduce costs, and enhance scalability. Several works focus on resource-efficient LLMs by exploring core methods such as pruning, quantization, and distillation. Studies in [[6](#bib.bib6), [19](#bib.bib19)] highlighted these methods as foundational strategies for minimizing computational overhead while maintaining accuracy. These techniques reduce the size and complexity of LLMs, making them more accessible for deployment in real-world scenarios. Similarly, [[5](#bib.bib5)] extended this discussion by addressing the challenges of designing lightweight architectures and accelerating inference. The authors in [[20](#bib.bib20)] provided a broader view, examining efficiency strategies across the entire LLM lifecycle, from training to deployment.

Energy efficiency is another critical aspect explored in the literature. Some works [[21](#bib.bib21), [4](#bib.bib4)] emphasized the importance of developing environmentally conscious LLM deployment strategies and discussed methods for reducing the energy footprint of LLM inference. These works emphasized hardware-aware optimizations, distributed inference techniques, and sustainable AI practices, particularly for edge and mobile deployments. LLM inference is not your normal deep learning model deployment nor is it trivial when it comes to managing scale, performance and COST. Understanding how to effectively size a production grade LLM deployment requires understanding of the model(s), the compute hardware, quantization and parallelization methods, KV Cache budgets, input and output token length predictions, model adapter management and much more.

If you want to deeply understand these topics and their effects on LLM inference cost and performance you will enjoy this talk.

This talk will cover the following topics:

Why LLM inference is different to standard deep learning inference
Current and future NVIDIA GPU overview - which GPU(s) for which models and why
Understanding the importance of building inference engines
Deep recap on the attention mechanism along with different types of popular attention mechanisms used in production
Deep dive on KV Cache and managing KV Cache budgets to increase throughput per model deployment
Parallelism (reducing latency) - mainly tensor parallelism but data, sequence, pipeline and expert parallelism will be highlighted
Quantization methods on weights, activations, KV Cache to reduce engine sizes for more effective GPU utilization
Increasing throughput with inflight batching and other techniques
Detailed performance analysis of LLM deployments looking at Time to first token, inter-token latencies, llm deployment characterizations, and more that can help reduce deployment costs
The main inference engine referenced in the talk with TRT-LLM and the open-source inference serve NVIDIA Triton.

# LLM Inference vs Traditional Inference | 6-Minute Crash Course with Robert Nishihara
## Linda Vivah
5870 subscribers
107 likes

### Description
2154 views
Posted: 5 Mar 2026
Walk with Robert Nishihara & I in NYC with 10% charge as we talk through 5 key differences between 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗩𝗦 𝗥𝗲𝗴𝘂𝗹𝗮𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲…. let’s see how much we can get through before our mic dies! 🪫🗽🤣

With regular machine learning models you can just take an input, run a single forward pass, and spit out an answer…

Like a vision model gets an image → runs once → says “cat.”

𝗟𝗟𝗠𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝗻’𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁.

They generate one token at a time, so the whole inference process is way more dynamic — and that’s why they need specialized engines like vLLM, SGLang, or TensorRT-LLM.

Here’s what makes them different 👇

1️⃣ 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘂𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗯𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴
Regular models process fixed-size batches.LLMs? Every prompt and response is a different length. So we use continuous batching -nconstantly sliding new requests into the GPU as others finish, so nothing sits idle.

2️⃣ 𝗧𝘄𝗼 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀 (𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗹 + 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲)
First, the model “reads” your prompt (prefill), then it writes its answer one token at a time (decode). The prefill step is heavy on compute, the decode step is bottlenecked by memory - so they’re often scheduled separately to keep throughput steady.

3️⃣ 𝗧𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸𝘆 𝗚𝗣𝗨 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁
LLMs reuse parts of previous conversations to respond faster - that’s the KV cache.Managing this cache (what to keep, evict, or move) is hard, and systems like vLLM’s PagedAttention exist just to handle that efficiently.

4️⃣ 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗳𝗶𝘅-𝗮𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴
If two prompts start the same way (“Once upon a time…”), you don’t want to re-compute that prefix every time. LLM servers can cache those shared prefixes so new queries reuse existing computation … kind of like autocomplete with memory.

5️⃣ 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 & 𝗠𝗶𝘅𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘁𝘀 (𝗠𝗼𝗘)
Some newer LLMs use Mixture of Experts. Instead of running every feed-forward layer for every token, they have many “expert” versions and only activate the most relevant ones. It’s like having a huge team of specialists, but only calling the ones you need for that moment.

Watch the video to join us on a tech talk vlog style in the NYC streets … NYC chaos and all 📹 😂

### Transcript:
Hey Robert, so what's the difference between LLM inference and regular inference? Well, there's so many important differences between LLM inference and regular inference. Yeah, I mean there's a reason you have specialized inference engines like VL SG Lang, TensorRT LLM, and so forth. To start off with, large language models do variable length computation, right? You have variable length inputs, you have variable length outputs. That's very different from say a traditional convolutional neural network that you might use for computer vision where you have a fixed size image input and are doing a fixed amount of computation and then generating a some label as your output, right? What's hard about variable length computation? Well, one of the most important techniques for getting good performance out of inference is batching, right? You don't want to just process one item or one data point at a time, you want to process a batch of items at a time because the overhead is not linear. It's not that much more expensive to process two inputs than it is to process one input. So, you want to do a bunch of them at a time to get good performance. But, if you are batching your requests and each one requires a different amount of computation, some are going to finish earlier, some are going to finish later. # The Engineering Guide to Efficient LLM Inference: Metrics, Memory, and Mathematics

![Burak Degirmencioglu](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*wapNJg5665AQhn-aKL94pQ.jpeg)

Listen

The deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) presents a fundamentally different engineering challenge than model training. While training is a massive exercise in raw compute power, usually bound by FLOPs, inference is a nuanced battle against memory bandwidth. Understanding this distinction is the first step toward building production-grade systems that are both cost-effective and responsive.

![]()

## **Key Takeaways**

**Pre-Inference Optimization:** While this guide focuses on serving models efficiently, the battle for speed often begins during training. If you are customizing models for specific domains, optimization starts with the dataset and training method. To understand how training decisions impact downstream performance, read our guide on [**Advanced LLM Finetuning Techniques**.](https://medium.com/ai-in-plain-english/a-practical-guide-to-advanced-llm-fine-tuning-from-lora-to-qlora-462b01f44022)

## What Performance Metrics Actually Matter in Production?

Before optimizing, we must define success. In an engineering context, vague notions of “speed” are insufficient. We rely on specific, quantifiable metrics derived from production constraints to measure the efficacy of an inference engine.

![]()

## LLM Metrics: Defining Latency and Throughput

There are four primary metrics that provide a granular view of performance:

### **Latency**

In LLM inference, **Latency** is defined as the total time required to complete a full request cycle. It combines the initial processing time and generation time, calculated as:

![]()

### **Throughput**

The total number of output tokens generated per second across all concurrent requests.

**The Engineering Trade-off:** Minimizing latency usually requires low batch sizes to process a single request as fast as possible. However, maximizing throughput requires high batch sizes to saturate the GPU’s compute capabilities, which invariably increases queue times and individual request latency.

![]()

## Bottleneck Analysis: Using the Roofline Model

To scientifically identify whether a specific layer in your model is stalling due to memory access or computation limits, we utilize the Roofline model. This model helps visualize the upper bound of performance based on the hardware’s peak throughput and memory bandwidth.

### What is Arithmetic Intensity?

The core metric for the Roofline model is Arithmetic Intensity, defined as the ratio of floating-point operations to data movement:

![]()

Tools like **“LLM-Viewer”** have been introduced to automate this analysis. They profile individual layers to determine their specific FLOPs counts and memory access patterns, allowing engineers to visualize exactly where the model falls under the “roofline” of the hardware.

## Why is the KV Cache Critical for Long Contexts?

The single most significant factor in handling long context windows and large batch sizes is the efficient management of the [**Key-Value (KV) cache**](https://medium.com/towards-artificial-intelligence/the-secret-behind-fast-llm-inference-unlocking-the-kv-cache-9c13140b632d). In the attention mechanism, the model computes Key and Value tensors for every token.

### How Does Caching Work?

During the prefill phase, we compute and store these tensors:

![]()

If we did not cache these values, the decoding phase would require re-computing the attention map for the entire previous sequence to generate every single new token, resulting in quadratic complexity. By caching them, we turn decoding into a linear operation regarding the sequence length.

However, this comes at a cost. The memory footprint of the KV cache grows linearly with both sequence length and batch size. For long-context models, the KV cache can easily exceed the size of the model weights themselves, leading to **Out Of Memory (OOM)** errors. To mitigate this, engineers employ **KV Cache Quantization**, which reduces the precision of the stored tensors (e.g., from FP16 to INT8), significantly lowering memory bandwidth usage without catastrophic accuracy loss.

**Deep Dive(Suggestion):** The size of the KV Cache is dictated by the model’s underlying architecture. Modern architectures utilize variants like Grouped Query Attention (GQA) and Sliding Window Attention (SWA) to reduce this memory footprint fundamentally. For a technical breakdown of these architectures, check out our article on the [**Attention Mechanism for LLMs**](https://medium.com/ai-in-plain-english/how-did-attention-mechanisms-revolutionize-large-language-models-8498bb606ef8).

## How Do We Engineer System-Level Optimization?

Moving from a naive implementation to a high-performance serving engine requires specific algorithmic and system-level interventions.

### Can We Solve the Straggler Problem?

In static batching, the GPU waits for all sequences in a batch to finish before processing the next batch. If one sequence is short and another is long, the GPU cycles are wasted waiting for the “straggler.”

**Continuous (or Dynamic) Batching** solves this. Instead of waiting for a batch to complete, the scheduler injects new requests immediately as previous ones finish specific tokens. This creates a fluid stream of execution that dramatically improves throughput.

![]()

### How Does Quantization Impact Inference Speed?

Quantization involves reducing the precision of weights and activations, for example, from 16-bit floating point to 8-bit integers (INT8). Referring back to the Roofline model, this technique directly improves **Arithmetic Intensity** by reducing the denominator (Bytes). Since less data needs to travel from memory, memory-bound operations (like decoding) see immediate speedups.

Further optimizations include **Operator Fusion**, where multiple kernels (such as MatMul followed by Bias and ReLU) are combined into a single kernel execution to minimize memory round-trips. Additionally, for distributed systems like Spark, **Fractional GPU Allocation** allows multiple tasks to share a GPU, maximizing utilization.

**Beyond Basic INT8:** While standard quantization is effective, advanced techniques are required to maintain accuracy at lower precisions (like 4-bit). Methods like GPTQ, AWQ, and SmoothQuant offer different trade-offs between calibration time and inference speed. # [Literature Review] Scaling LLM Inference with Optimized Sample Compute Allocation

The paper "Scaling LLM Inference with Optimized Sample Compute Allocation" by Kexun Zhang et al. presents OSCA (Optimizes Sample Compute Allocation), a novel algorithm aimed at improving the efficiency of inference time operations in large language models (LLMs) by optimizing the distribution of compute resources allocated to various sampling configurations.

### Introduction

At the core of many inference-time algorithms for LLMs lies the sampling operation, which is critical for generating outputs, particularly in tasks like code generation and reasoning. The central challenge addressed in this paper is the effective allocation of compute resources when sampling outputs from different configurations (models, temperatures, etc.). The authors argue for the necessity of a mixed allocation strategy, as various problems may require different configurations for optimal performance.

### Methodology

Problem Formulation

The authors formalize the allocation problem as a learning task, where the goal is to distribute a fixed compute budget (C) across multiple sampling configurations (H). Each configuration produces a certain probability of generating a correct solution for a given problem.

* Given a set Dtest​ of problems and a compute budget C, the sampling configurations comprise different hyperparameters (e.g., model type, temperature, and output language). The allocation can be a pure allocation (all compute on one configuration) or a mixed allocation (budget spread across multiple configurations).

Optimization Objective

The primary objective is to maximize the expected pass rate (pass@C), which is defined as the probability of at least one successful sample being generated under the compute constraints:

Pr(problem xj​ solved with Ci​ samples from hi​)=1−i=1∏∣H∣​(1−pij​)πi​

where pij​≈C0​cij​​ is the estimated probability of success for configuration hi​ on problem xj​, and πi​ denotes the compute allocated to configuration hi​.

OSCA Algorithm

The OSCA algorithm works through the following steps:

1. **Estimation of Pass Probability**: The algorithm begins by estimating a probability matrix P based on the performance of different configurations on a training set. Specifically, pij​ is computed by sampling C0​ times from hi​ for each xj​.
2. **Iterative Optimization**: OSCA utilizes a hill-climbing approach, which begins with a randomly initialized allocation of compute and iteratively explores neighboring allocations to find a better one by maximizing the expected pass rate. This process repeats until no improvements can be found:

   * Each neighbor is formed by adjusting the current allocation slightly (incrementing one configuration while decrementing another).

### Evaluations and Results

The authors perform extensive experiments on two benchmarks (LiveCodeBench and LiveBench) involving multiple tasks to evaluate OSCA's performance across various compute budgets.

1. **Performance Comparison**: OSCA is consistently shown to outperform both default pure allocations and uniform mixed allocations. Notable improvements include:

   * 128 times less compute on code generation tasks compared to optimal pure allocation.
   * 25 times less compute on reasoning tasks.
2. **Agentic Workflows**: The benefit of OSCA extends beyond single-turn tasks, impacting multi-step processes as observed in SWE-Bench. The results indicate significant reductions in compute while maintaining or improving performance.
3. **Ablation Studies**: The authors examine the influence of different hyperparameters on the allocation effectiveness, identifying which configurations benefit most from mixed allocations. They demonstrate that the learned allocation strategies remain robust even with smaller training datasets and estimation budgets.

### Key Insights

One of the primary insights from the paper is the contrasting effectiveness of mixed allocations compared to pure allocations. The authors showcase that a uniformly mixed allocation (where compute is evenly spread across all configurations) does not perform optimally in all scenarios, illustrating the necessity for an approach like OSCA.

### Conclusion

The paper concludes that OSCA significantly advances the ability to efficiently allocate compute resources for sampling operations in LLM inference. Its implications stretch across various complex workflows, making it a substantial contribution towards optimizing the usage of large language models in practical applications.

Overall, the detailed description of OSCA and its testing reflect its potential as a valuable tool for enhancing model performance while being mindful of computational efficiency, which is especially crucial in resource-constrained environments.

# [Literature Review] Inference Scaling vs Reasoning: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal LLM Problem-Solving

The paper titled "Inference Scaling vs Reasoning: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal LLM Problem-Solving" by Marwan Abdelhameed and Pavly Halim from New York University addresses the growing complexities in the development of large language models (LLMs), particularly the conflicting objectives of enhancing reasoning capabilities while maintaining computational efficiency.

### **Core Methodology Overview**

The methodology outlined in the paper focuses on the implementation and empirical analysis of two prominent techniques: Quiet-STaR (Self-Taught Reasoner) and REBASE (REward BAlanced SEarch), followed by an exploration of their integration. The researchers specifically utilized the Mistral-7B model and the GSM8K dataset to benchmark their findings.

**1. Quiet-STaR (Self-Taught Reasoner)**

**Key Innovations:**

* **Parallel Generation:** Quiet-STaR employs an algorithm that efficiently generates rationales for token predictions by creating attention masks that allow tokens to reference relevant previous tokens seamlessly.
* **Meta-Tokens:** It introduces learned start-of-thought and end-of-thought tokens that orchestrate rationale generation, ensuring the model maintains context and coherence while reasoning.
* **Mixing Architecture:** A shallow multi-layer perceptron (MLP) is used to interpolate between predictions that involve reasoning and those that do not, allowing a gradual transition for the model to incorporate rationales into its outputs.
* **Non-myopic Learning:** The model is designed to learn from multi-token sequences rather than relying on solely immediate token predictions, thereby capturing more extensive semantic relationships and improving reasoning accuracy.

The operational functionality of Quiet-STaR is structured into three stages:

1. **Think:** Generating the rationales concurrently across all tokens.
2. **Talk:** Mixing base predictions with rationales through learned weights adjusting the degree to which each influences the output.
3. **Learn:** Using reinforcement learning to refine rationale generation based on the improvements seen in predictions.

**2. REBASE (REward BAlanced SEarch)**

**Innovative Approaches:**

* **Node Quality Rewards:** Unlike traditional Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), REBASE uses a reward model to score the quality of nodes immediately, circumventing the extensive computational demands of rollouts while ensuring high-quality paths are prioritized.
* **Balanced Exploration:** This algorithm balances node expansion based on a softmax-normalized reward model, enabling exploration of promising paths without neglecting overall path diversity.
* **Resource Efficiency:** By focusing computational resources on the most promising paths, REBASE achieves notable gains in efficiency, with particularly strong results when employing smaller models.

**Integration of Quiet-STaR and REBASE**

The integration seeks to leverage the depth of reasoning provided by Quiet-STaR alongside the speed and efficiency from REBASE. Key considerations during integration include:

* **State Synchronization:** Establishing unified state representations that effectively coordinate reasoning steps with search processes.
* **Resource Management:** Dynamic control of resource allocation for reasoning and search, fine-tuning to maximize computational efficiency without sacrificing reasoning depth.

**Experimental Protocol**

The experimental setup involved:

1. **Model Configuration:** Usage of the Mistral-7B model with specific context lengths, retaining standard transformer architecture.
2. **Datasets:** The GSM8K dataset, which includes rigorous mathematical reasoning challenges, serves as the assessment barometer.
3. **Performance Assessment Variables:** Several key metrics were employed to evaluate outcomes, including accuracy per TFLOP (floating-point operations), accuracy per second, and a composite efficiency score.

### **Results and Insights**

**Performance Metrics:**

* **Quiet-STaR:** Exhibited the highest accuracy (32.03%) but with significant computational costs (12.73T FLOPs, 554.66s runtime).
* **REBASE (with varying tree widths):** Offered improved efficiency, particularly at a width of 3 (601.14 efficiency score) while maintaining baseline-level accuracy (10.94%).
* **Integration of Both Methods:** Saw an unexpected performance drop with an accuracy of 9.38%, moderate resource requirements, and increased latency.

**Key Findings:**

* **Optimization Conflict:** The research unveiled inherent tension between Quiet-STaR's expansive reasoning paths and REBASE's pruning strategy, leading to integration challenges.
* **Resource Competition:** The two methods struggled to efficiently share computational resources, which hindered the effectiveness of the combined approach.

### **Conclusion and Future Directions**

The findings underscore significant discrepancies when merging these two methodologies, highlighting the need for new architectures that can harmonically balance reasoning depth with computational efficiency. Recommendations for future research include exploring adaptive control mechanisms and broader exploration of reasoning domains beyond mathematical problems to enhance scalability and efficiency in LLMs.

This detailed methodology provides a comprehensive framework for assessing the interplay between reasoning and computational efficiency in the evolution of large language models, laying the groundwork for future innovations in AI and machine learning contexts.

# LLM Inference Computational Complexity

Updated 12 July 2025

* LLM inference is characterized by high computational and memory costs, largely due to self-attention mechanisms that scale quadratically with input sequence length.
* Research actively reduces these costs using model compression, system-level optimizations like dynamic batching, and efficient key-value cache management.
* Adaptive routing and specialized hardware further enhance scalability by dynamically matching queries to the most cost-effective model or processing resource.

The computational complexity of [LLM inference](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/llm-inference) refers to the theoretical and practical measures of resource consumption (in terms of operations, memory, latency, and energy) required to generate outputs from LLMs. As model sizes and application demands have increased, minimizing the asymptotic and constant factors of inference cost has become central to scalable and efficient LLM applications. Current research reveals a diverse landscape of algorithms, system strategies, hardware techniques, and adaptive [multi-model orchestration](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/multi-model-orchestration) for addressing these challenges.

## 1. Theoretical Foundations and Key Complexity Drivers

The dominant source of computational complexity in modern LLM architectures is the [self-attention mechanism](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/self-attention-mechanism) of Transformer models, where the computational and memory costs often scale quadratically with input sequence length n: O(n²) in the prefill phase and O(n) per token during incremental decoding ([Zhen et al., 28 Apr 2025](/papers/2504.19720)). For an L-layer, h-head, d-dimensional model, a representative formula for a single attention layer is: MHA(Q,K,V)=Softmax(QKT/dk​​)⋅V The overall runtime and memory footprint is thus critically dependent on the sequence lengths, batch sizes, number of layers and heads, and the degree to which key/value caching, weight sharing, and compression are used.

In resource-constrained or high-throughput scenarios, the complexity must further account for hardware platform characteristics—including memory bandwidth, cache architecture, and data movement overheads, which can dominate wall-clock inference times even when FLOP counts are fixed ([Chitty-Venkata et al., 2024](/papers/2411.00136)).

## 2. Model Compression and System-level Optimization

Reductions in computational complexity are pursued at both the model and system levels ([Chavan et al., 2024](/papers/2402.01799)).

* **[Model Compression](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/model-compression):** Structured and unstructured pruning (LLM-Pruner, FLaP), quantization (LLM.int8(), GPTQ, AWQ, QLoRA, OmniQuant), and low-rank approximations decrease the number of active parameters and memory footprints. For example, 4-bit quantization can reduce weight and runtime memory up to 70% with negligible perplexity increase. Unstructured techniques apply sparsity by setting weights below a threshold τ to zero:

Empirical results show that these methods can dramatically lower cost, though aggressive compression without fine-tuning may harm model quality ([Chavan et al., 2024](/papers/2402.01799)).

* **System-Level Techniques:** Memory-management methods (paged attention, cache offloading), GPU parallelism (tensor/pipeline parallelism ([Zhen et al., 28 Apr 2025](/papers/2504.19720)), as well as dynamic re-sharding ([Su et al., 9 Mar 2025](/papers/2503.06433))), and operation fusions ([FlashAttention](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/flashattention-fa), custom kernels ([Wu et al., 2023](/papers/2401.05391))) further optimize inference runtime. FlashAttention and similar fused kernels reduce redundant memory access, exploit tiling, and efficiently use caching, decreasing the number of kernel launches and bandwidth demand.

## 3. Adaptive Routing and Multi-LLM Hierarchical Inference

Recent multi-model routing and hierarchical inference (HI) strategies decrease effective complexity by dynamically matching queries to the simplest adequate model ([Bae et al., 2023](/papers/2312.11511), [Behera et al., 6 Jun 2025](/papers/2506.06579)). The system maintains a set

M={M1​,M2​,...,MK​}

with increasing cost and capability. A routing function R(q) maps input query q to an optimal model based on learned scoring functions over computational cost factors (including FLOPs, memory, energy, latency, financial implications, scalability, and input modality compatibility): R(q)=Mk​wherek=fR​(q,θ) Hierarchical inference chains queries through progressively larger models, accepting early outputs if a [confidence](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/confidence) score threshold is met: M(q)={M1​(q),​if s1​(q)≥τ1​ M2​(q),​if s1​(q)<τ1​ and s2​(q)≥τ2​ … MK​(q),​otherwise​ ComplexityNet, for example, improves resource use by 90% via automatic task complexity estimation and routing, with accuracy maintained above 86% ([Bae et al., 2023](/papers/2312.11511)). [Multi-LLM routing](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/multi-llm-routing) frameworks benchmarked in ([Behera et al., 6 Jun 2025](/papers/2506.06579)) leverage unified [efficiency metrics](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/efficiency-metrics) such as the Inference Efficiency Score ([IES](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/injected-external-squeezing-ies)): IES(q)=C(Mk​)α⋅Q(q)+(1−α)⋅R(q)​ where Q(q) is quality, R(q) is responsiveness, and C(M\_k) is the composite cost.

## 4. Dynamic Batching, Scheduling, and Length Prediction

Through [dynamic scheduling](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/dynamic-scheduling) and batching, redundant computations and “tail latency” in batched inference can be greatly mitigated ([Zheng et al., 2023](/papers/2305.13144), [Zhen et al., 28 Apr 2025](/papers/2504.19720)). [Response length perception](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/response-length-perception) enables micro-batching queries with similar predicted output lengths, minimizing wasted computation on idle tokens. For instance, batched queries with diverging response lengths traditionally produce up to 66% redundant computation due to stragglers. Variable Batch Size ([VBS](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/necklace-like-vortex-bound-state-vbs)) sets the batch size by: B=L0​B0​×L​ where B0​ is batch size at reference length L0​, and L is the predicted response length. Failure Collection and Recomputation (FCR) further reduces waste by identifying outliers for secondary processing. These advances achieve up to 86% higher throughput in production-like settings ([Zheng et al., 2023](/papers/2305.13144)).

Memory usage and computational cost are significantly influenced by how key-value (KV) caches are structured and maintained.
